discussion_comments.comment_body: [P2] Make capability transfer explicit. A matching name such as hook.beforeTool does not mean two clients enforce the same policy, and custom tools with the same name can have different contracts. Selecting the first attached registrant can silently change a running task's behavior. Please require an explicit compatible takeover contract, or fail clearly for capabilities that cannot safely transfer.

Done in b9871407b6: I removed the fallback entirely. Requests only go to the client that built the run. If that client has disconnected or detached, the request fails with "The app running this task disconnected before it could respond. Send a message to continue." Nothing is transferred or replayed. Each case emits `task.capability_owner_gone` (`reason`: `disconnected` | `detached` | `cancelled_while_waiting`) so we can track how often it happens.

discussion_comments.comment_body:
🟡 **security** (medium)

The `state` parameter is no longer enforced on the auth callback, only used to decide whether to show a confirmation prompt. Combined with the corresponding change in AuthService.ts (`private readonly _authNonce = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("hex")` — a value now generated once per extension lifetime and never rotated), the state check no longer provides any anti-forgery/replay protection: a previously observed or attacker-constructed auth URL remains valid for the whole session, and a forged callback (`<scheme>://saoudrizwan.claude-dev/auth?token=...`) only requires the user to accept one dialog to bind the extension to an attacker-controlled account. The old code rejected mismatched states outright.

**建议**: Keep the convenience path for external sign-ins but restore a real security boundary, e.g. (a) regenerate/rotate the nonce per auth request and accept a state that is a member of a short-lived, bounded set of recent nonces rather than a single lifetime constant, and/or (b) make the confirmation prompt explicitly describe the risk ("this sign-in request could not be verified — continue only if you started it") and default to cancel. At minimum, document why the state check is intentionally downgraded so it is not mistaken for CSRF protection.

**证据**: `if (authService.authNonce !== state) {`

*high*

`cwd` is granted read-write with no check, and `keep-changes-in-project-extension.ts` seeds `allowedRoots` from `options.cwd` the same way. The safety boundary is therefore whatever directory the session started in: from `~`, all of `~` is writable (I verified this on macOS); from `G:\`, the whole drive. Suggest resolving real paths and failing closed, with a message, when any read-write grant is a volume or filesystem root, the home directory, or an ancestor of it.

*low*

On darwin `/dev/null` is not writable inside the sandbox: `echo hi > /dev/null` exits 1 with `/dev/null: Operation not permitted`, and the tool result carries the "outside your project" note. Model-authored commands redirect there constantly. Add `/dev/null` to the darwin grants.

Valid. `addRemoteServer` built the invalid-URL error from the env-expanded URL, and Bun's URL parse error also echoes its input, so any error message can embed a credential-bearing URL. Fixed: the MCP error now echoes the URL as entered (with the `${env:…}` placeholder), and in production every URL inside a logged error message, cause, or error-like object is reduced to its origin (`redactUrlsInText` in `apps/vscode/src/utils/redact-url.ts`). Covered by `McpHub.addRemoteServer.test.ts` and the new URL cases in `Logger.test.ts`.

Update: the free-text URL scrubber described above was later removed (see the discussion on the long-scheme thread). The fix for this finding is the source change alone: `addRemoteServer` echoes the URL as entered, never the env-expanded value.

Valid. Parentheses and brackets are legal URL characters, so ending the match there left the rest of the URL in the log. The matcher now ends only at whitespace, quotes or angle brackets. It trims trailing sentence punctuation and closing brackets with no opener inside the URL, so `(see https://x/y)` still reads cleanly and `http://[::1]:3000` is kept whole. Everything else in the match is redacted together. That change also rewrote the trailing-punctuation trim as a linear loop, which covers the CodeQL alert. Covered by the new cases in `redact-url.test.ts`.

+/**
+ * Reduces a URL to its origin for log output. Paths, query strings and
+ * fragments routinely carry OAuth state, authorization codes, reset tokens and
+ * API keys (some MCP servers embed the key as a path segment); userinfo can
+ * carry credentials. Unparseable input is replaced entirely rather than echoed.
+ */
+export function redactUrlForLog(url: string): string {
+	try {
+		const parsed = new URL(url)
+		if (parsed.origin === "null") {
+			// Non-hierarchical and file schemes (mailto:, data:, file:, ...): keep only the scheme.
+			return `${parsed.protocol}<redacted>`
+		}
+		return parsed.origin
+	} catch {
+		return "<invalid url>"
+	}
+}
+
+// A scheme followed by `//`, up to whitespace, a quote or an angle bracket.
+// Parentheses and square brackets are valid URL characters (and brackets
+// delimit IPv6 hosts), so they must not end a match. The scheme length is
+// bounded so scanning stays linear.
+const URL_IN_TEXT = /\b[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]{0,31}:\/\/[^\s"'`<>]+/gi

Right, and this is the pattern with scrubbing arbitrary error text: it's a blocklist, and there's always another shape (schemeless URLs, bearer tokens, keys in plain text). So the free-text scrubber is removed rather than extended.

The policy is now: in production, extra arguments get the same trust as the log message itself, which production has always logged verbatim. A call site that builds an error message out of a secret is a bug at that call site. The one found here is fixed at the source: `addRemoteServer` echoes the URL as entered, with `${env:…}` placeholders, never the expanded value (covered by `McpHub.addRemoteServer.test.ts`). The only other URL this PR logs, the "Opening browser:" line, is reduced to its origin at that call site.

Valid. V8 (and Bun) quote the parsed input in `JSON.parse` errors, e.g. `Unexpected token 's', "sk-live-…" is not valid JSON`, and this isn't limited to `parseApiKeys`: any parse of a settings file or credential-bearing response would leak the same way. Fixed in the Logger by error type rather than per call site: in production a `SyntaxError` (including one in a `cause` chain) logs only its name. The zod `APIKeySchema.parse` errors in the same function are fine as is: zod 4 issue messages carry paths and keys, not values. Covered by the new JSON-parse case in `Logger.test.ts`.

Following symlinks here is intentional: bun's node_modules/.bun layout is symlinks, and people link sibling checkouts into a workspace. The reader runs as the user, for the user's own UI (now gated to the trusted desktop connection, see the thread above), so a link resolving outside the root shows the user a file they already own and can open in their editor from the same panel. Rejecting resolved targets would break legitimate trees without closing a real boundary, so I am leaving this as is and documented the intent on assertInsideRoot.
Fixed in 8a327a6: only '..' itself and '../' / '..\\' prefixes are rejected now, with a test for a '..notes' directory.

The sensitive-file list is narrow. It misses `.netrc`, `.pgpass`, `.pypirc`, `.aws/credentials`, `*.keystore` and service-account JSON, and it only matches filenames. Since this pushes dirty untracked files, a broader or shared list seems worth having.

Expanded the sensitive-path checks to include `.netrc`, `.pgpass`, `.pypirc`, `.aws/credentials`, `*.jks`, and `*.keystore`. Regression tests cover these paths and sensitive files in unpublished history, including files deleted in a later commit. This addresses the listed filename gaps, but it remains filename-based protection: service-account JSON under an arbitrary filename is not detected.

discussion_comments.comment_body:
Addressed. `setRuleDisabledInFrontmatter` now takes the allowed roots for the scope (global Rules directory, or the workspace `.clinerules` directory or single file), resolves the request path through symlinks with `realpath`, requires a regular file inside one of those roots, and only writes the file types the SDK loader reads (`.md`, `.markdown`, `.txt`, or the bare `.clinerules` file). Anything else keeps the extension-state toggle only. Tests cover the symlink escape, non-rule files in a rules folder, and relative or missing paths.

For context on severity: the RPC caller is the extension's own webview, the same trust level as the existing skill toggle and rule create/delete handlers, so the practical risk was corrupting a stray non-rule file that happened to live in a rules folder. That is what the containment and extension checks close.
